attributes.nuance_translation: A phrase that expresses when someone thinks that they are resolved to do (A).

attributes.body:
The combination of a verb with the auxiliary verb う, or よう, followed by the う-Verb 思（おも）う gives us the common expression ようと思（おも）う. This expression is often translated as 'I think I will (A)', or 'I shall (A)'. It is also close to the casual expression 'I'm gonna (A)'.

Remembering that う and よう can have one of three possible meanings in Japanese (as discussed in the よう grammar point), ようと思（おも）う is usually only used to express one of those three. That 'one' is as follows:

意志（いし） - Expresses intentions (has a similar meaning to ～するつもりだ).

This expression is also often used with 思（おも）っている. In these cases, it highlights that the intention of the speaker is something that they regularly think, or have been thinking about for some time.

思（おも）っている may also be used when describing the intentions of another person, as discussed in our lesson about と思（おも）う.

Caution

Let's be careful to remember the difference between the auxiliary verbs よう, and ようだ. They are different constructions that have different meanings, and behave in unique ways grammatically.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar
Minna no Nihongo II Main Textbook (beginner)
Minna no Nihongo English Translation and Grammatical Notes

attributes.description: Volitional + と思う vs. Volitional + と思っている
The many faces of よう
All uses of volitional form and よう explained

attributes.body: 〜よう・おうと思う uses the volitional form with と思う to express plans or intentions, like 'I intend to (A)' or 'I'm thinking of doing (A)' In contrast, plain と思う expresses a simple thought. For example, この本を読もうと思います means 'I intend to read this book.', while この本は面白いと思います means 'I think this book is interesting.'.

first_relatable.slug: ようと思う-おうと思う
first_relatable.title: 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う
first_relatable.meaning: I think I will, I think I shall, Going to, Gonna (Volitional + と思う)

attributes.body: Both use the volitional Verb [よう] form. On its own, it expresses a suggestion, e.g. 食べよう ('Let's eat.'). When combined with と思う, it expresses an intention or plan, e.g. 食べようと思う ('I'm thinking of eating.'). The key difference is that Verb [よう] includes others in the action, while ～ようと思う expresses the speaker's personal intent.

first_relatable.slug: ようと思う-おうと思う
first_relatable.title: 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う
first_relatable.meaning: I think I will, I think I shall, Going to, Gonna (Volitional + と思う)

attributes.body: Both つもりだ and 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う can both be used to express intentions or plans for the future. つもりだ feels slightly more 'official' or definite, similar to the English 'I intend to' or 'I hope to'. In contrast, 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う has a more casual and less definitive feel, similar to the English 'I'm thinking of (doing something)'.

first_relatable.meaning: To plan to, To intend to

second_relatable.title: 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う
second_relatable.meaning: I think I will, I think I shall, Going to, Gonna (Volitional + と思う)

attributes.body: 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う expresses intention, similar to 'I'm thinking of doing X,' e.g. 行こうと思います ('I plan to go.') てみる conveys the idea of trying something to see what it's like, e.g. 行ってみる ('I'll go and see.'). These forms can be combined, e.g. 行ってみようと思います ('I plan to go and see what it's like.')
